blurb: Dr. K hosts the finale: ADAM — the agentic system that uses BOTH LM and FinBERT, plus an LLM as adjudicator. Six layers, three evidence agents, six discrepancy diagnoses — and preliminary results you must read with the label on.
intro: Dr. K saved the real idea for last — well, almost last: one episode follows this one, and it is about the study itself. ADAM doesn't pick a winner between LM and FinBERT — it keeps their disagreement, diagnoses it, and hands you a decision. This episode, you become the adjudicator. And remember: every number here is preliminary. Validation is ongoing, and honest science says so on the label.

body: ADAM — An Agentic Decision Support System for Financial Narratives, by Kazim Topuz, Jessica Bedson, Tally Ferguson, and Thomas Kim (University of Tulsa, DSI 2026) — is built on one idea: preserve disagreement, diagnose it, and turn it into decision-relevant evidence. It is not a three-vote ensemble, and it is not “an LLM does everything”. It is six layers, three specialized evidence agents, and an adjudicator that reasons about their evidence.

The six layers: 1 — Disclosure & Decision Context (10-K Item 1A / Item 7, firm / year / section / sector); 2 — Structuring & Contextualization (section extraction, paragraph objects, prior-year / peer links); 3 — Three Specialized Evidence Agents (LM, FinBERT, Context & Quality); 4 — Intelligent Adjudication (assess convergence, diagnose conflict, retain ambiguity); 5 — Disclosure Intelligence Synthesis (paragraph → section → company-year measures); 6 — Decision-Support Outputs (profiles, alerts, drill-down, explanations).

The three agents are deliberately non-equivalent. The LM lexicon agent gives transparent, auditable word evidence — Positive / Negative, Uncertainty, Litigious, Constraining, Modal — but is context-blind. The FinBERT agent gives finance-domain contextual sentiment — P(Negative), P(Neutral), P(Positive), predicted class, confidence — but with lower traceability. The Context & Quality agent does not decide sentiment at all: it qualifies informational significance — persistence / novelty, peer similarity / distinctiveness, specificity, boilerplate, hedging / negation / caution. The outputs stay separate until adjudication.
lessons.h: ADAM: six layers, three agents, one adjudicator
lessons.tip: Agentic here does not mean every component is an LLM. It means specialized roles, structured evidence, and explicit coordination. If someone calls ADAM “just an LLM”, ask them where the Context & Quality evidence lives.

body: The adjudicator separates what other systems collapse. It returns separate fields: linguistic sentiment (Positive / Negative / Neutral), economic direction (Favorable / Adverse / Mixed / No clear direction), informativeness (High / Medium / Low), and status — confidence, ambiguity, review needed. A sentence can be linguistically neutral, economically adverse, and highly informative, all at once — and ADAM is designed to preserve those distinctions.

When the agents disagree, the adjudicator diagnoses why, using six primary discrepancy categories: No meaningful conflict; Lexical–semantic mismatch; Boilerplate / generic language; Factual event vs neutral wording; Conditional / negated / mixed language; Unresolved evidence. Market outcomes are not observed by the adjudicator — they are reserved for external validation.

A worked disagreement (illustrative passage): “The company is not expected to face a material loss from the pending litigation this year.” LM says NEGATIVE — it matched the list words “loss” and “litigation”. FinBERT says NEUTRAL — it read “not expected to” as negation. The adjudicator's diagnosis: conditional / negated language — the disagreement is resolvable once the negation is seen, and the paragraph is not the distress signal LM's count suggests.

How hard is the underlying task? The human reference set — 300 paragraphs (144 Item 1A, 156 Item 7, 2016–2025, all 11 sectors), each reviewed independently by 3 blinded reviewers — shows it is genuinely difficult: unanimous agreement was only 21% for sentiment, 25% for economic direction, and 32% for informativeness. Most of the rest had a two-of-three majority. Disagreement here is not annotation noise — it is a signal of task difficulty.
lessons.tip: Agreement does not guarantee correctness, and disagreement does not necessarily imply ambiguity. The adjudicator's first question is always: do the signals converge — and if not, what explains the conflict?

body: Every number in this lesson is labelled PRELIMINARY — VALIDATION ONGOING: the evaluation uses the 300-paragraph human reference set, and confirmatory testing, confidence intervals, and paired significance tests are still to come in the final paper.

Linguistic sentiment accuracy: LM 37.3%, FinBERT 60.7%, LM–FinBERT ensemble 58.7%, ADAM 82.7%. Macro-F1: LM 0.320, FinBERT 0.529, ensemble 0.384, ADAM 0.745. Economic direction: ADAM 83.3% accuracy, macro-F1 0.689. Disclosure informativeness: ADAM 71.4% accuracy, macro-F1 0.607 — the hardest of the three constructs, and the one with the most room to improve.

The key analysis is disagreement. LM and FinBERT disagree on 162 of 300 paragraphs (54%). There, ADAM reaches 76.5% accuracy (macro-F1 0.703), vs FinBERT 68.5% (0.606), ensemble 64.8%, and LM 25.3%. And on the 77 paragraphs where both base models were wrong, ADAM is correct on 89.6%.

The ablation asks whether the architecture matters or the LLM does all the work — same adjudicator, progressively more evidence. Informativeness macro-F1: Judge-only (paragraph only) 0.453 → Base evidence (paragraph + LM + FinBERT) 0.469 → Full ADAM (+ Context & Quality) 0.607. The gains are Δ +.138 vs Base and +.154 vs Judge-only, both statistically significant. But be honest about the rest: for sentiment, Judge-only already reaches 82.0% (vs Full ADAM 82.7%), and for economic direction Judge-only reaches 84.0% — slightly above Full ADAM's 83.3%. The architecture matters most where the construct depends on information outside the focal paragraph: prior filings, peer language, persistence, novelty, specificity.

Decision support is the payoff, not the accuracy. ADAM's High-informativeness flag: 81.0% precision, 69.9% recall — vs a simple FinBERT-negative rule at 19.5% precision for High informativeness (the proxy trap). Confidence routing: confidence below 0.80 sends 56% of paragraphs to review, captures 92.3% of ADAM's sentiment errors, and accuracy on the automated remainder rises to 97.0%. The DSS value is selective attention + traceability + review routing — not simply a higher sentiment score.

game.done: LM matched a negative word, FinBERT read the negation — and you diagnosed it instead of averaging it away. That is adjudication.

lessons.tip: The most important number on this page is not 82.7%. It is the label above it: PRELIMINARY. A decision-support system that hides its uncertainty is selling false precision — the exact failure ADAM was built to avoid.

outro: You can now read the results — but can you explain how they were earned? One episode left: the study itself. The research questions, the nested tests, and why holding the adjudicator constant is the whole trick.

quiz.why: ADAM is an agentic system: it coordinates heterogeneous evidence through six layers and an adjudicator — it is explicitly not a three-vote ensemble, and “agentic” means specialized roles plus structured evidence and explicit coordination, not that every component is an LLM.

FinBERT beats LM on sentiment (60.7% vs 37.3%)
quiz.q: In the ablation test, what proves the architecture itself matters — rather than the LLM doing all the work?
quiz.why: Holding the adjudicator constant, adding Context & Quality evidence lifts informativeness macro-F1 from 0.453 to 0.607 — the architectural gain, and it is significant. For sentiment and direction the judge alone already does most of the work (82.0% / 84.0%), so the honest claim is task-dependent: the architecture matters for informativeness.

quiz.q: ADAM's High-informativeness flag has 81.0% precision. What does the simple FinBERT-negative rule achieve for High informativeness — and what does that show?
quiz.why: The FinBERT-negative rule reaches only 19.5% precision for High informativeness, vs ADAM's 81.0% (with 69.9% recall). Negative tone is a bad proxy for “this paragraph matters” — which is exactly why ADAM separates sentiment from informativeness instead of collapsing them.
